question: What is the effect of an exposure when unmeasured confounders cannot be adjusted away?

lousdal2018.cite: Lousdal (2018). An introduction to instrumental variable assumptions, validation and estimation. Emerging Themes in Epidemiology 15: 1.
lousdal2018.checked: every quote read word for word in the Europe PMC full text (PMC5776781) on 20 Nov 2026; places are its section headings; in-text reference numbers are left out

steps.title: Find an instrument
steps.text: Look for something that pushes people towards the exposure but has no other route to the outcome, like a coin toss in a trial.

quotes.text: An instrument is defined as a variable that predicts the exposure, but conditional on exposure shows no independent association with the outcome. The instrument affects the outcome solely through the effect on exposure.

steps.title: Relevance
steps.text: The instrument must really change the exposure. This one can be checked in the data.

quotes.text: The relevance assumption: The instrument Z has a causal effect on X.

steps.title: Exclusion
steps.text: The instrument may reach the outcome only through the exposure. This has to be argued, not tested.

quotes.text: The exclusion restriction: Z affects the outcome Y only through X.

steps.title: No shared causes
steps.text: Nothing that causes the outcome may also cause the instrument. A real coin toss guarantees it; a natural one has to be defended.

quotes.text: The exchangeability assumption: Z does not share common causes with the outcome Y

steps.title: Divide
steps.text: Divide the instrument's effect on the outcome by its effect on the exposure. A fourth assumption (homogeneity or monotonicity) says whose effect this is.

quotes.text: Intuitively, the numerator corresponds to the intention-to-treat effect of the causal effect of assignment on outcome
The denominator is a measure of compliance with the assigned exposure.

confounding.text: If a suitable instrument can be identified, the causal average effect among compliers may be estimated even in the presence of unmeasured confounding.

model-assumptions.text: The three basic assumptions allow for identification of an upper and lower bound of the causal effect

low-power.text: Often natural variation only gives rise to a weak association between instrument and exposure.

exercise.title: Why not just compare the exposed?
exercise.intro: Each simulated person has a hidden trait U that makes them both more likely to take the exposure X and better off on the outcome Y. A coin Z nudges some people towards X. Compare the naive estimate with the instrument's ratio.

quote.text: When non-compliance increases, the denominator shrinks and inflates the diluted intention-to-treat estimate in order to estimate the causal effect had everyone complied.

exercise.data_label: Example data, simulated for this exercise with a seeded random generator.
exercise.model: Model: X = 1 when 1.2·U + nudge·Z + noise > 1; Y = 1·X + 2·U + noise; U and noise are standard normal; Z is a fair coin. The nudge is 2 (strong) or 0.25 (weak).

limits: Angrist, Imbens & Rubin (1996), the card's reference, was not read in this task; the steps follow Lousdal (2018).
Angrist & Krueger (1991), the card's example, was not read in this task.
The exercise's effect is the same for everyone, so the ratio targets that single effect; with varying effects it estimates the average effect among compliers (Lousdal 2018, Background).
